text.p: It is impossible to know all of the factors involved in the economic slowdown in Japan but pessimism over the future in that country is unwarranted, U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan said Thursday.
Responding to a question during testimony before the Senate Finance Committee, Greenspan emphasized elements of strength in Japan's economic history.

"There is something different about the way the Japanese have managed to create a society in which their inflation rate is negligible, their unemployment rate is very low and, until very recently, their growth rate has been really quite impressive," Greenspan said.
"Their history suggests that their pessimism at this stage is probably being grossly overdone," he added.
The Fed chairman did point to some demographic issues in Japan that are concerning people there.
Like the United States, Japan is confronting a dilemma over how to support an aging population, Greenspan said.
However, he said that projections point to more rapid increases in the average age of the Japanese population.
"Whatever problems we have, theirs are far more severe," Greenspan said.
